en: [SaSū(C) 0] May there be well-being! Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
[SaSū(C) 1] Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagṛha.
On Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great community of monks— namely,
twenty-two thousand monks— such as the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
4. and with the Venerable Śāradvatīputra, 5. and with the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, 6. and with the Venerable Rāhula;
7. and with the venerable Bakkula, 8. and with the venerable Bhadravāsa, 9. and with the venerable Bhadraśrī;
10. and with the venerable Nandaśrī, 11. and with the venerable Jāṅgula, 12. and with the venerable Subhūti.
13. and with the Venerable Revata, 14. and with the Venerable Nandasena, 15. and with the Venerable Ānanda;

16. With these twenty-two thousand bhikṣus as their leaders, and with sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas, such as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya; [SaSū(C) 3] 2. namely, with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya and others.
3. and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, 4. and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumāraśrī, 5. and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumāravāsin;
6. and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumārabhadra, 7. and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Anūna, 8. and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
9. and by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, 10. and by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sudarśana, 11. and by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja;
12. With these sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas as their leaders, and with sixty-two thousand sons of gods, such as the son of god Arjuna; [SaSū(C) 4] 1. and the son of god Arjuna; 2. and so forth.
3. by the divine son Bhadra, 4. by the divine son Subhadra, and 5.
by the divine son Dharmaruci;
6. and by the divine son Candanagarbha, 7. and by the divine son Candanavāsin, 8. and by the divine son Candana;
9. With these as their leaders, there were sixty-two thousand sons of gods.
[1] And with eight thousand celestial maidens, [2] namely, the celestial maiden Mṛdaṅginī and [3] the celestial maiden Prāsādavatī; and so forth.
4. by the celestial maiden Mahātmasaṃprayuktā, 5. by the celestial maiden Varṣaśrī, and 6. by the celestial maiden Padmaśrī;
7. by the celestial maiden Prajāpativāsinī, 8. by the celestial maiden Balinī, and 9. by the celestial maiden Subāhuyuktā;
10. Together with eight thousand celestial maidens headed by these;
and with eight thousand nāga kings, such as the nāga king Apalāla; 1. and so forth.
3. by the nāga king Elapatra, 4. by the nāga king Timiṅgila, and 5. by the nāga king Kumbhasāra;
6. by the nāga king Kumbhaśīrṣa, 7. by the nāga king Sunanda, and 8. by the nāga king Suśākha;
9. And by the nāga king Gavaśīrṣa; 10. with these eight thousand nāga kings as their leaders.
[SaSū(C) 7] They all went toward the great city of Rājagṛha, toward Vulture Peak Mountain, and toward where...

The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, approached them; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and stood before him.
And the Blessed One signaled his acceptance by remaining silent.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

1. "O Blessed One, many tens of millions of gods, many tens of millions of apsarases, many tens of millions of bodhisattvas, and many tens of millions of śrāvakas have gathered and are seated here to hear the Dharma. 2. Therefore, O Blessed One, I would ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain matter."

“If the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to answer the questions I ask. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra: “Sarvaśūra, you have my permission to ask whatever question you desire for your constant practice. Ask, Sarvaśūra, whatever you wish; I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every question you ask.”

4. When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, is there a discourse on the True Dharma which, upon being heard, causes the five deeds of immediate retribution of all sentient beings to be extinguished without remainder, and likewise causes other karmic obstructions to be exhausted?"
"And how do they swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter. Therefore, Sarvaśūra, listen well and attend closely."
"I shall speak to you.
"So be it, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One then said this to him:
Sarvaśūra, there is a Dharma discourse called the *Saṃghāṭa*;
it shall circulate in Jambudvīpa at this time. Sarvaśūra, whoever shall hear this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma discourse, their five actions of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) will be completely exhausted.
3. And they shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
What do you think, Sarvaśūra, regarding one who hears this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*?
“Would that being produce as much a mass of merit as the mass of merit of a single Tathāgata?
“Sarvaśūra, it should not be viewed in this way.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
"But how, Blessed One, should it be viewed?
The Blessed One replied:
"It is like the mass of merit of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā."
Sarvaśūra, those beings will produce such a mass of merit as those who hear this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*,
all of whom shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
4. All shall behold the Tathāgata, and all shall become those who have seen the Tathāgata; 5. and all shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
6. They shall become invincible to Māra, the Evil One;
7. and they shall all attain wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma), O Sarvaśūra, who hear this *Saṃghāṭasūtra*.
They will all know arising and cessation.

Then, at that time and on that occasion, all those millions of gods, nāgas, humans, and apsarases rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and all questioned the Blessed One.
2. "Blessed One, how great is the mass of merit of a single Tathāgata?
[SaSū(C) 18] 1. The Blessed One said:
"Listen, son of good family, to the measure of the mass of merit of a single Buddha. 2. It is, for example, like the drops of water in the great ocean."
Suppose there were as many atoms as there are in Jambudvīpa, and suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā,
and all of them were bodhisattvas established in the ten stages;

And as for the mass of merit belonging to those bodhisattvas, the mass of merit of a single Buddha is even greater than that. Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, those beings who hear this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse will produce a mass of merit even greater than that.

As long as it is not possible to reach the limit of that mass of merit through the application of calculation. 4. Sarvaśūra, at that time, at that moment, having heard these words, there will be great enthusiasm... [SaSū(C) 19] 1. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, who are those beings that will be thirsty for the Dharma?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
“Sarvaśūra, there are these two types of beings who are thirsty for the Dharma. Which two?”
Namely, Sarvaśūra, the first is one whose mind is equal toward all sentient beings;
the second, Sarvaśūra, is one who, having heard the Dharma, proclaims it equally to all sentient beings.
Sarvaśūra the Bodhisattva said:
“Blessed One, having heard what Dharma do all sentient beings achieve equal illumination?
The Blessed One said: “O Sarvaśūra, having heard a single Dharma, one dedicates it toward awakening.”

And when one dedicates [merit] toward awakening, then all sentient beings will become thirsty for the Dharma. 3. Second, O Sarvaśūra, he who plunges into the Mahāyāna is always thirsty for the Dharma.
[SaSū(C) 21] Then those tens of millions of gods, nāgas, humans, and apsarases rose from their seats, stood before the Blessed One with palms joined, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“O Blessed One, we are parched with thirst for the Dharma; may the Blessed One fulfill our hopes and those of all sentient beings.
Then, at that moment, the Blessed One manifested a smile. Then...
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Blessed One,
and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for manifesting this smile?"
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:

"Sarvaśūra, all those beings who come here shall all fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they all attain perfection for the sake of perfecting the range of activity of the Tathāgatas."
[SaSū(C) 24] 1. The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
“Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that these beings, having come here, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening?
2. The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter. Here, Sarvaśūra, a distinction in dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is to be seen.

Once upon a time, Sarvaśūra, in the past, incalculable eons ago, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnaśrī—one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world."

The unsurpassed charioteer of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, at that time I was a young brahmin. And those beings who are currently established by me in the knowledge of a Buddha were all, at that time and on that occasion, deer.
They existed. At that time and on that occasion, I made this vow:

"May all those deer who are currently tormented by suffering be reborn in my buddha-field, and may I establish them all in the knowledge of a Buddha. And those deer, having heard those words, spoke these words:
"So be it. Sarvaśūra, by that root of merit, these beings, having come here, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then, having heard this encouragement from the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what will be the lifespan of those beings?"
2. The Blessed One said: "The lifespan of those beings will be eighty eons.
1. The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
“Blessed One, what is the measure of an eon? The Blessed One said:
“Listen, son of good family.”
For example, Sarvaśūra, suppose a certain man were to cause a city to be built, twelve yojanas in length and breadth, and three yojanas in height.
3. And one should fill that city completely with sesame seeds;
4. then, after the passing of a hundred years, that man should take a single sesame seed from that city filled with sesame seeds and cast it outside;
by this method, that man would bring all those sesame seeds to exhaustion.
And that city would be without root and without foundation;
yet even now, the eon would not have been exhausted.
Furthermore, Sarvaśūra:
2. It is as if there were a mountain, measuring twenty-five yojanas in extent and twelve yojanas in height;
3. Then suppose some man were to build a house on the side of that mountain;
4. after the lapse of a long period of a hundred years, he were to wipe it once with a cloth from Kāśī;
by doing this, there might come to be the exhaustion of that mountain.
And yet, the eon would not be exhausted. Such, Sarvaśūra, is the measure of an eon.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and—
Placing his right knee upon the ground and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
2. "By this single dedication, O Blessed One, one generates such a vast mass of merit that, namely, for eighty eons the measure of one's lifespan will be happiness.
3. What need is there to mention one who will perform even greater service within the teaching of the Tathāgata?
1. The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family."

Whoever hears this *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra, their lifespan shall be eighty-four thousand eons. How much more so, Sarvaśūra, will that being who writes down the *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra produce a far greater mass of merit? Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, whoever with a clear mind and deep resolve pays homage to the *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra, they shall remember their past lives for ninety-five eons in every birth.
4. For sixty thousand kalpas he will be a universal monarch (cakravartin);
in this very life, Sarvaśūra, he will be beloved by all.
6. Sarvaśūra, he shall not meet his end by means of a weapon.
No *kākhorda* demon shall overcome him;
and at the time of death, he shall see ninety million Buddhas face to face.
And all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, O Sarvaśūra, will comfort him, saying:
"Do not fear, virtuous man!

Since you have heard this well-spoken *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, this great Dharma-discourse, such a mass of merit has been produced by you. Furthermore, those ninety-five billion Buddhas in their respective world-systems will each grant you a prophecy."
11. "What need is there to mention, Sarvaśūra, one who shall hear this *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, this great Dharma-discourse, in its entirety and in detail?
1. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, I shall hear this *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, this great Dharma-discourse."
"Blessed One, how great a mass of merit shall I produce?
The Blessed One said:
"As great as is the mass of merit of as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges."
“Sarvaśūra, that being will produce such a mass of merit.
Sarvaśūra the Bodhisattva said:
“Blessed One, as I listen to this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*...”
“Blessed One, I do not perceive satiety. The Blessed One said:
“Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra! It is well that you do not perceive satiety regarding the dharmas. I too, Sarvaśūra, do not perceive satiety regarding the dharmas;
how much less, Sarvaśūra, could foolish ordinary people perceive satiety?”
1. Any son of good family or daughter of good family, Sarvaśūra, who shall produce faith in the Mahāyāna, will not go to a state of ruin for a thousand eons.
2. For five thousand eons, they will not be reborn among the animals.
3. For twelve thousand kalpas, he will be of evil intellect;
4. for eighteen thousand kalpas, he will not be reborn in the border regions;
5. for twenty thousand kalpas, he will be a hero in giving.
6. He will be reborn in the worlds of the gods for twenty-five thousand kalpas;
7. he will practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for thirty-five thousand kalpas;
8. he will live as one who has gone forth from the household life for forty thousand kalpas.
9. For fifty thousand kalpas he will be a bearer of the Dharma; 10. for sixty-five thousand kalpas he will cultivate the recollection of death;
11. for that son of good family or daughter of good family, Sarvaśūra, no evil karmas whatsoever shall be experienced.

12. Furthermore, Māra, the Evil One, shall find no opportunity against him, nor shall he ever again be reborn in a mother’s womb. 14. O Sarvaśūra, those who hear this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* will, wherever they are reborn, not fall into the lower realms for ninety-five incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). 15. For eighty thousand eons, they shall be retainers of what they have heard (*śrutadhara*).
16. For one hundred thousand kalpas they will abstain from taking life;
17. for ninety-nine thousand kalpas they will abstain from false speech;
18. for thirteen thousand kalpas they will abstain from malicious speech. 19. Those beings, Sarvaśūra, who shall hear this Dharma-discourse are rare to find.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat,
draped his upper robe over one shoulder,
and placed his right knee upon the ground.
Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was,
he said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how great will be the mass of demerit produced by those beings who reject this Dharma-discourse?"
3. The Blessed One said:
"Sarvaśūra, one will produce a vast mass of demerit by rejecting the true Dharma.
1. Sarvaśūra said:
"Blessed One, how great will be the mass of evil karma of sentient beings?
The Blessed One said:
"Enough, enough, Sarvaśūra."

"Do not ask me about the mass of my evil karma. Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, if one were to give rise to a malicious mind toward as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges rivers, and if another were to reject this Saṃghāṭa Sūtra, [the latter would incur a greater transgression]."

This person will produce an even greater mass of evil and unwholesome karma than that. Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, those who harbor a mind of malice toward the Mahāyāna will produce an even greater mass of unwholesome karma; Sarvaśūra, those beings are truly burnt beyond recovery.
Sarvaśūra said:
"How, Blessed One, can those beings be liberated?
The Blessed One said: "It is just so, Sarvaśūra."

3. "For example, Sarvaśūra, suppose some man were to cut off the head of a certain being, and then someone else were to anoint it with some medicine—whether he should smear that head with honey, or sugar, or molasses, or ghee, or oil. 4. Sarvaśūra, would it be possible for that being to be raised up again?
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
"It is not possible, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Sarvaśūra:"
It is just as if there were a second person who,
with a sharp weapon, would strike another being;
yet he would not be able to deprive that being of life with a single blow.
Moreover, Sarvaśūra, although a wound may arise for him,
if he then applies the proper medicinal treatment, he is liberated from that wound.
When he is thus liberated, he then remembers his suffering.
"I now know that I shall never again perform any sinful or unwholesome karmic formation.
In this very way, Sarvaśūra, when that person remembers the suffering in hell, he completely abandons all evil.
2. Then he will bring all dharmas before him;

3. having brought all dharmas before him, he will bring all wholesome dharmas to fulfillment. 4. Just as, for example, Sarvaśūra, when a man has died, his mother and father grieve and lament, yet they are not able to save him.
5. In this very way, Sarvaśūra, foolish ordinary beings are unable to accomplish their own welfare or the welfare of others, like parents who have lost all hope;
6. in this very way, Sarvaśūra, those beings become hopeless at the time of death.
[SaSū(C) 41] 1. "Sarvaśūra, these two beings are hopeless. Which two?
Namely, one being who commits evil karma or causes it to be committed; and a second who rejects the true Dharma (*saddharma*). These two beings are hopeless at the time of death.
[SaSū(C) 42] 1. The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
"Venerable Blessed One, what is the destination of those beings, and what is their future state?
The Blessed One said:
Sarvaśūra, the destiny of those beings who reject the true Dharma is infinite;
their future state is infinite:
for an entire eon, Sarvaśūra, they shall experience painful sensations in the Raurava great hell.
4. for one kalpa in Saṃghāta, 5. for one kalpa in Tapana, 6. for one kalpa in Pratāpana.
7. One eon in the Kālasūtra great hell; 8. one eon in the Mahāvīci great hell;
9. one eon in the Romaharṣa great hell.
10. For one *kalpa* in the Hahava great hell. 11. Sarvaśūra, in these eight great hells, sentient beings who reject the true Dharma must experience suffering for eight *kalpas*.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One:
"It is suffering, Blessed One; it is suffering, Sugata. I do not venture to hear it."
2. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
(1) Why do you not venture to hear this speech, so full of great terror? Beings experience sensations in the hells, joined with suffering.
Whatever wholesome action one performs, happiness will be its result;
whatever unwholesome action one performs, suffering alone will be its result.
(3) For one who is born, death is suffering; there is grief, and then the suffering of bondage.
Indeed, suffering is constant for the fool who does not understand the cause of happiness.
(4) Indeed, those wise ones who remember the offerings made to the Buddha,
and who have faith in the Mahāyāna, shall not go to an evil rebirth.
(5) In this very way, Sarvaśūra, impelled by past karma,
even a small deed performed results in a vast fruit to be experienced.
Just as one who sows a small seed obtains an abundant fruit,
so too is the seed truly sown in a Buddha-field, which is an excellent field.
(7) The wise find happiness; they delight in the teaching of the Jina;
they avoid evils and perform much that is wholesome.
(8) Those who shall give even a particle as small as an atom in charity within my teaching will,
for eighty thousand eons, possess great enjoyments and great wealth.
(9) Wherever they are reborn, they always remember their giving;
for thus is this profound offering to a Buddha of great fruit.
[SaSū(C) 44] 1. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, how should the Dharma be understood within the teaching of the Blessed One?
Blessed One, how will the root of merit be grasped after hearing this *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra, this discourse on the Dharma?"
The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, if someone were to serve Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges rivers with all the requisites for happiness,
and another were to hear this Dharma discourse, the Saṃghāṭasūtra, their mass of merit should be known to be exactly equal."
[SaSū(C) 45] 1. The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
"Blessed One, how should the fulfillment of the roots of merit be accomplished? When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Sarvaśūra, whatever is a root of merit, that should be known as equal to the Tathāgata. 3. Sarvaśūra said:
"And what, Blessed One, is the root of merit that should be known as equal to the Tathāgata?
The Blessed One said:
"Sarvaśūra, the Dharma-preacher is to be known as equal to the Tathāgata. Sarvaśūra said:
"Who, Blessed One, is a Dharma-preacher?
The Blessed One said: "He who causes the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* to be heard is a Dharma-preacher."
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
“Blessed One, those who hear this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, will produce such a mass of merit;
what need is there to mention those who write it down or recite it?”
"Blessed One, how great a mass of merit will they produce?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Sarvaśūra."

For example, suppose that in each of the four directions there were Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, equal in number to the sands of twelve Ganges rivers, who remained for twelve kalpas equal to the sands of twelve Ganges rivers and taught the Dharma;
and suppose they were to describe the mass of merit of this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, for one who writes it down— it would not be possible to reach the limit of that mass of merit.

Or even to express it with speech: (3) even by forty-eight Buddhas, Blessed Ones, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, it would not be possible to express that mass of merit belonging to one who writes [this]; (4) what need is there to mention those who will cause it to be read, or who will contemplate it?
Or those who will be meditators on the Dharma.
Sarvaśūra the Bodhisattva said:
"Blessed One, how much of a heap of merit will they produce by reciting it?"
2. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
(1) Whatever merit there is in reciting even a single four-line verse, [it is equal to the merit of honoring] as many Victors as there are grains of sand in eighty-four Ganges rivers.
(2) Even if those who have recited it here were to describe the merit [thereof] while remaining steadfast,
that merit would not be exhausted until the final prophecy is reached.
(3) Suppose eighty million Buddhas were to remain for as many eons as there are [in that number],
praising all the virtues of the Mahāyāna throughout the ten directions.
And whatever merit belongs to the *Saṃghāṭa*, that shall never come to an end;
thus, the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas is indeed difficult to encounter and infinite.
Furthermore, at that time and on that occasion, eighty-four hundred thousand koṭis of sons of gods approached the Tathāgata and the exposition of the Dharma-discourse known as the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*.
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence, they said this to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! It is well that such a treasury of Dharma has been established by the Blessed One in Jambudvīpa."
(49) 1. Eighteen thousand million Nigranthas approached the place where the Blessed One was; having approached, they...
They spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Victory, O Śramaṇa Gautama!
The Blessed One said:

"The Tathāgata is always victorious. O Nigrantha heretics, how is there victory for you heretics? They replied, "May the ascetic Gautama be victorious, may he indeed be victorious! The Blessed One said:
"I do not see victory for you. And he said:
(1) "You stand in error; how can there be victory?
Listen, O Nirgranthas, I shall speak for your benefit."
(2) There is no happiness for one of childish intellect; what victory will there be for you? They do not know the path, so what victory will there be for them?
I shall show you the profound path with the eye of a Buddha.

[SaSū(C) 50] 1. Then those Nirgranthas, being angry in the presence of the Blessed One, gave rise to a mind of ill-will. 2. At that time, on that occasion, Śakra, the lord of the gods, struck his thunderbolt. [SaSū(C) 51] 1. Then those eighteen koṭis of Nirgranthas—

Terrified, trembling, and afflicted by great suffering and dejection, they wept with choked voices. And the Tathāgata caused his own self to disappear from view. Then those Nirgranthas, their faces bathed in tears, [continued to weep].
Not seeing the Tathāgata, they spoke this verse:
(1) "There is no protector here at all, neither mother nor father likewise;
we see only this forest, with its empty dwellings and no refuge."
There is indeed no water, nor trees, nor birds;

[SaSū(C) 252] 1. Then, about five thousand young beings rose from their seats, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

by it we are bound in saṃsāra, not knowing its end."
(2) We do not recognize the path, nor is the path itself seen;
we have become like the blind, O Protector—please take us under your care.
(3) We entreat you, O Hero, Leader: teach us the Dharma!
For we were born with little wisdom and are indeed ignorant of happiness.
(4) Teach us the Dharma and liberate us from this terrible suffering;
wherever we may be reborn, may there be for us the sight of a Buddha.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena approached those young beings;
having approached them, he—
He said this:
(1) "Eat your food, drink the wonderful broth;
afterwards, having become confident, you shall hear the Dharma without fear."
2. They said:
(2) "Venerable Elder, who are you? We do not know you.
We behold you as gracious, of peaceful appearance, and of great renown."
(3) You are liberated from the great terrors of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of hungry ghosts; all your evils have been stilled, so that you shine resplendent in the world.
(4) We see in his hand a water-pot endowed with the seven jewels,
and a jewel-encrusted thread wound around his body, which is a mass of radiance.
(5) We are unable to carry out your words, which are so peaceful;
we have no need for food, nor even for delicious drink.
(6) From food, excrement arises, and likewise urine from drink;
blood comes from the nutrient essence (*rasa*), and from blood, flesh is produced.
(7) We have no need for food, nor for drink prepared with spices; nor do we require fine garments made of silk and woven cloth.
(8) Bracelets should not be made of gold, nor should they be made of pearl strings;
one should not even make finger-rings, for all of these are subject to impermanence.
(9) We desire life and that we not go to an evil rebirth; we seek the gift of Dharma, not even the pleasures of the gods.

(10) One should cultivate the state of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), not the sovereignty of universal monarchs (cakravartin); for even universal monarchs will die, leaving behind their most beautiful continents.
(11) Sons do not follow behind, nor do wives or daughters;
even the seven treasures are turned back, for they shall not go behind him.
(12) Having assembled a great multitude, they shall not fall behind;
they do not run ahead, nor do they again fall under the sway [of distraction].
(13) Kings who have been deluded by constant [desire] throughout many lifetimes,
having committed sinful deeds, fall into the Raurava hell.
(14) Having wandered in the four directions with the seven great and powerful jewels,
where will that supernatural power go when she dwells in the Raurava hell?
(15) Once dead, they are unable to exercise supernatural power where no ground exists.
O Elder, listen to us: go where the Tathāgata is.
(16) We long for a sight of him, just as a mother and father do; for we have no mother, no father, and no brothers.
(17) That very Tathāgata is the teacher of the world, as well as its mother and father;
he alone is both the moon and the sun, the one who reveals the path to security.
(18) For he is the liberator from cyclic existence, by whom one is not born again; he is not a ferryman across the flood, nor across the great terror of the flood of afflictions.
(19) By him sentient beings were led across so that they no longer turn back;
by him the True Dharma was taught, which reveals supreme enlightenment.
(20) We have no need for food, nor do we desire the fruits of sovereignty; we, who fear hell, have no business with going to the world of the gods.
(21) A human birth where an omniscient one is seen is considered happy;
yet those with short lifespans are also seen, due to their own misdeeds.
(22) They are attached to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and do not perceive death;
they do not understand and they do not fear, being deprived of the knowledge of cessation and arising.
(23) Those whose minds are overcome by ignorance do not know subtle phenomena, they do not perform subtle actions, and they do not know the peaceful realm.
(24) Passing away, they do not grow weary, being born again and again;
for a long night, struck by suffering, they are constantly beaten by the rod of impermanence.
(25) They will seize the property of others and be subjected to slaughter and imprisonment;
bound by the fivefold bonds, they are impelled by their former sins.
Despairing and pierced by the arrows of grief, they will die;
as their consciousness ceases, they will lament piteously.
(27) Who indeed might be my protector? I shall give away all my enjoyments—gold, silver, and crystal—and I shall even become a slave.
(28) "I shall perform every task worthy of a servant;
I have no need for royal enjoyments, nor for grain, nor for wealth."
(29) "I have need of my own body; an evildoer is not released [from it].
For in this way, O Elder, there would be no food for us."
(30) Even kings will die, though they have partaken of exquisite food;
even the sons of gods will die, though they have drunk the most excellent nectar.
(31) Having brought before him refined food and drink endowed with various flavors, the king touched the meal with his tongue.
(32) For kings, greedy for flavors, commit no small amount of evil;
they take delight in fleeting tastes wherein no essence is found.
(33) We must not drink, nor indeed must we eat;
such is the nature of our duty, so that we may be liberated from suffering.
We have gone for refuge to that Buddha, who is liberated from the bond of craving, who brings liberation from the affliction of craving, and who is freed from all bonds.
(35) For we go for refuge to the Great Sage, the Lord of the World;
we go to pay homage to him whose appearance is dear to all beings.
(36) "We do not know your name; tell us your auspicious name.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena said:
(36) "Indeed, you wish to hear the name of every person."
(37) Surrounded by nine hundred thousand koṭis of beings, the Tathāgata was thus attended.
They said:
(37) "We wish to hear your name, which arises from all virtues."
(38) "It is heard that your name is profound, you who are a disciple of the Buddhas. He said:
(38) "I am Bhaiṣajyasena by name; indeed, I am the medicine for sentient beings."
(39) I shall teach you all the supreme medicine for every person afflicted by disease, which pacifies all ailments.
(40) Passion is a disease, a great disease that perishes dreadfully in the world; delusion is a most terrible disease, by which those lacking wisdom wander about.
(41) Beings seized by hatred go to hell, and likewise to the realms of animals and hungry ghosts; how can there be peace for these fools?
6. They said:
"Having heard this auspicious Dharma, may we be liberated from all suffering;
yet those of childish intellect and ignorant minds remain unliberated from all sufferings."
(43) Free from evil deeds, we shall hear the gift of Dharma;
having abandoned all evil, our fears and terrors have been eliminated.
(44) We shall soon behold the Perfectly Awakened One, the liberator from all diseases,
the King of Physicians, the Great Physician, the healer of those who suffer.
(45) Go quickly, Elder, to pay homage to the Tathāgata; and in our name, offer salutations to the Guide of the World.
(46) Quench this disease; extinguish this most terrible fire!
This entire body is ablaze, and though being consumed, it is not stilled.
O you of noble vows, show compassion for us who are tormented by suffering;
the burden of the body is a great burden, a sharp and most dreadful weight.
(48) Overcome by hatred and delusion, people always carry [these burdens]; being ignorant, they repeatedly pass through the gateway to liberation.
(49) They do not realize that they must die, and yet no fear arises; being ignorant of the path to liberation, they do not see the path to liberation.
(50) "We shall never die"—thinking thus, they remained complacent; yet, utterly bewildered, they did not realize it even as they beheld their mother dead.
(51) Others do not remember their fathers, being constantly afflicted by disease;
agitated by afflictions and karma, how can they eat food?
(52) We do not know the end of suffering; we labor in vain.
Such sufferings as ours arise from birth and ignorance as their cause.
(53) Great fear and heavy burden are perception, mental formations, and feeling;
the fool who does not understand the Dharma is made to wander by craving.
For one born into this world for the sake of misfortune, burdened by the weight of a physical body,
there is need for bathing and ointments, as well as clean and most beautiful clothing.
One should prepare delicious food that is pleasing to the body,
and likewise cause the five musical instruments to be played in a manner that is delightful to the ear.
(56) Their eyes are stained by forms arising from the seven precious gems, and their tongue craves every kind of delicious and refined flavor.
(57) The body always longs for a soft and subtle touch; pleasure arises when two pieces of flesh are pressed together by the body.
(58) For this body is indeed insentient; who could find delight therein? Yet my feet find pleasure there because it is covered with beautiful hide.
(59) At the time of death, neither clothing nor ointments provide protection;
even the body itself will not be a refuge, so how much less clothing and ointments?
(60) It is called the Person (puruṣa); it enters the body as breath, possessing great strength and sharp power.
Through discernment, one perceives that [breath] as a great quality within that body.
(61) Previously, surrounded by horses and elephants, I was whirled about in play;
ignorant of the dharma of liberation, I delighted in evil deeds.
(62) Out of playfulness, I committed evil deeds without knowing of the next world; thus I have been born again and again, and have repeatedly encountered death.
(63) Grief is seen again and again, along with the bondage of lamentation;
the death of mothers has been witnessed, and fathers dead have also been seen.
(64) Kinsmen, sisters, sons, and even a wife who has died—all conditioned phenomena are indeed empty; for what conscious person would take delight in them?
(65) For, with a mind seized by greed, I did not recognize the peace of the Dharma unknown to me; I neither attained tranquility nor did I welcome death.
(66) Because my mind was shrouded by greed, I did not give that gift.
What evil could be equal to greed, which even today does not turn back?
(67) For we have become bewildered, and the entire world is bewildered; bewildered, we hear a sound that is the grasping of false dharmas.
(68) We seek liberation and meditations; we do not sustain this body.
May we become Buddhas for the sake of the world—teachers and guides for the universe.
The Buddha is the mother and father in the world; the Buddha is the one who reveals the path.
He rains down the rain of Dharma everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa.
(70) Deluded beings do not know how the gathering of dharmas occurs;
having directed the mind toward awakening, the gathering of dharmas is attained.
(71) All conditioned phenomena are empty; enjoyments and wealth are likewise empty. Having seen that the self is empty, we have become free from longing.
(72) Elder Bhaiṣajyasena, listen to our words;
we dismiss you to a distance for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
(73) Bodhisattvas, possessing vigor and great asceticism, do not grow weary;
remembering the faults of saṃsāra, they gather up virtuous qualities.
(74) Go where that Teacher is and ask on our behalf:
"Has the Teacher awakened in happiness? Does the Jina experience no distress whatsoever?"
(75) Māra has been defeated by you, along with his army and his mounts;
you have swiftly kindled the Dharma that brings happiness to all sentient beings.
(76) "Furthermore, we have not heard the Dharma by which we might become Buddhas; go quickly, O Elder, for the sake of our benefit."
(77) "We shall not rise until we behold the Tathāgata, who bears the thirty-two marks; all of us remain standing with reverence."
7. The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena said: "Look upward for a moment; what do you see right now?
Standing there, those five, no fewer than that, looked upward.
There were three hundred thousand gabled pavilions on all sides.
(80) Mounted upon the seven precious jewels and beautifully adorned with nets of gems,
there is a fully blossomed lotus in the center emitting divine fragrances.
(81) There they ask the Elder: "What is this that is seen here—these peaked pavilions with jeweled lattices, resting upon the filaments of lotuses?"
8. Bhaiṣajyasena said:
"These are your opportunities; go to behold the Buddha!
Pay homage to that Lamp of the World, who is the transcendent Teacher."
9. They said:
"We do not know, nor do we see, the path to the Tathāgata there;
since we do not know the path, where shall we go to pay him homage?"
10. Bhaiṣajyasena said: "One must go to pay homage to the Teacher, whose radiance is like nectar;
he cannot be grasped, just as infinite space cannot be grasped."
(85) This Teacher stands firm, just as the Meru mountains stand;
he may be compared to Sumeru and to the very depths of the great ocean.

(86) Because of his knowledge, which transcends the three-thousandfold world system, and because he is the source of all Buddhas, the Illuminator of the World is saluted by Bodhisattvas from the ten directions.
11. They said:
(87) "Look upon us, O Lord of the World; fulfill our aspiration! The Teacher has been saluted by us with our hearts; therefore, may we obtain the fruit thereof."

12. The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena said: "The Teacher is not attached to perfumes, nor to garlands, nor to ointments. He grasps the cause for the sake of sentient beings, by which they are liberated from the conditioned."
Māra cannot wage a most dreadful battle against him by whom the mind has been subdued and who has gone for refuge to the Buddha.
(90) He shall not fall under the power of death and will swiftly attain the dhāraṇīs;
having brought about clarity of mind, he then beholds the Teacher.

[SaSū(C) 254] 1. Then, the Tathāgata Kalaviṅkarutasvaramanojñaghoṣa manifested a smile. 2. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for manifesting this smile, that eighty-four thousand rays of light issue forth from the Blessed One’s mouth?
By those rays, the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system was filled with radiance,
and all thirty-two great hells were completely suffused."
5. And thirty-two celestial palaces were illuminated;
6. and those rays were of various colors, namely blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal, and silver;
7. and these rays, having issued from the Blessed One’s mouth, [proceeded].
Having provided every kind of comfort throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system,
and having returned once more, they circumambulated the Blessed One seven times.
They vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One:
“I would like to ask the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain matter.”
"If the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to answer the questions I ask. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
"Ask, Bhaiṣajyasena, whatever you desire; I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every question."
[SaSū(C) 256] 1. When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, thirty thousand koṭis of young beings have appeared. 2. They penetrate the subtle teaching of the Dharma of the Tathāgata. 3. Blessed One, the elder beings revile the subtle Dharma."
They revile them and oppress them, saying: "4. You are not beings who have grown old; you do not know the Dharma.
You are constantly attached to what is unrighteous and unwholesome. 5. Therefore, Blessed One, they speak words that are polished and pleasing. For what reason, Blessed One, do they speak such words?
6. The Blessed One said:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, do you not know for what reason these beings speak such words?
7. Having heard the Dharma spoken so gently and tenderly by the Tathāgata, Bhaiṣajyasena, they will thereby realize the meaning of all dharmas."
8. They shall be endowed with all virtuous qualities;
9. and they shall all penetrate the *dhāraṇī*. 10. From this day forward, they shall be established upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);
11. today they shall beat the great drum of the Dharma.
12. Today they shall become endowed with the great methods of the Dharma. 13. "Bhaiṣajyasena, do you see these gabled pavilions?
14. Bhaiṣajyasena said: "I see them, Blessed One."
"I see them, Sugata. The Blessed One said:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, these young beings today have ascended into these gabled palaces."
15. They will attain the realization of the Dharma;
16. today they will bring all wholesome qualities to fulfillment;
17. today they will beat the great drum of the Dharma.

18. Today there will be a realization of the Dharma for many classes of gods; 19. and for many beings who have set out toward rebirth in the hells, upon hearing this exposition of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, [there will be a realization of the Dharma].
There will be a complete defeat of all that turns away from saṃsāra.
At that very moment, ninety-nine hundred thousand billion aged beings attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala). They shall all be endowed with all dharmas;
and, Bhaiṣajyasena, they shall all be entirely freed from all suffering.
4. Bhaiṣajyasena, they will all accomplish the vision of all the Tathāgatas;
5. Bhaiṣajyasena, they will all be endowed with the Great Dharma. 6. Look around, Bhaiṣajyasena, in the four directions! 1.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena looked all around in the four directions.
2. From the eastern direction, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of fifty koṭis of Ganges rivers come;

3. from the southern direction, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty koṭis of Ganges rivers come; 4. from the western direction, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of seventy koṭis of Ganges rivers come.
5. From the northern direction, Bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of eighty *koṭīs* of Ganges rivers come;
6. from the downward direction, Bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ninety thousand *koṭīs* of Ganges rivers come;
7. from the upward direction, Bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of one hundred thousand *koṭīs* of Ganges rivers come.
8. And those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as they arrived one after another, bowed their heads at the feet of the Great Blessed One and stood to one side.
[SaSū(C) 259] 1. To the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who had come from the ten directions and were standing to one side, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena then said this to the Blessed One:
2. "Blessed One, what is this black form and red form that I see in the sky, in the atmosphere?"
3. The Blessed One said: "What is this, Bhaiṣajyasena?
Do you not recognize that which you see in the sky as a black form and a red form?"
4. He said: "I do not know, Blessed One; I do not know, Sugata. 5. The Blessed One said:
"Only this Tathāgata knows."

"Bhaiṣajyasena, this is Māra who has approached here for the purpose of causing blindness. Bhaiṣajyasena, do you wish to see these bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who are stationed in the midst of the sky? He replied: "I wish to see them, Blessed One;
I wish to see them, Sugata."
[SaSū(C) 260] 1. Then the Blessed One,
having shown those bodhisattvas,
addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
2. "Bhaiṣajyasena, bodhisattvas such as these, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, have arrived. 3. He asked:
"Lord, what is the cause, what is the condition, that so many of these bodhisattvas have come here?
4. The Blessed One said:
“Bhaiṣajyasena, by means of these young beings, all beings will come to possess the meditative concentration on the Dharma. 5. Do you see them, Bhaiṣajyasena?

Bodhisattvas possessing various powers of supernatural transformation have arrived. 6. I have beheld world-systems as numerous as the sands of a hundred billion Ganges rivers; therein I have seen bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Ganges rivers. 7. They abide each by their own power of supernatural transformation.”

They abide in various forms, with various colors, and with various strengths and configurations. Those bodhisattvas abide in the dwellings of the noble Dharma; those retinues of bodhisattvas abide in the dwellings of the Dharma.
The Blessed One spoke thus, and Sarvaśūra the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
Bhaiṣajyasena the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, both old and new, were filled with joy.
And that entire assembly, including the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. 3. 3. The Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saṃghāṭa* is completed.
